previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including end-stage renal disease, atrial fibrillation, and aortic stenosis was admitted for worsening shortness of breath over four days, associated with orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Imaging revealed a moderate right pleural effusion, which was drained via thoracentesis, leading to immediate symptom improvement. The effusion was transudative, likely due to congestive heart failure. She was found to have drug-induced pancytopenia, possibly from oral vancomycin used for recent C. difficile infection, and the antibiotic was discontinued early. Her warfarin was held due to an elevated INR of 3.1, and digoxin was stopped given a subtherapeutic level despite adequate rate control. She completed a hemodialysis session without complications and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, follow up on INR and CBC, and continue outpatient cardiac care.
problems: Other specified forms of effusion, except tuberculous
Intestinal infection due to Clostridium difficile
Mitral valve insufficiency and aortic valve stenosis

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ F with a history of ESRD on HD, HTN, atrial 
fibrillation on warfarin, who was admitted with worsening 
thrombocytopenia, in the setting of pancytopenia.

ACTIVE DIAGNOSES: 

# Thrombocytopenia/Pancytopenia: Mrs. ___ had had 
___ platelets for the last month, and upon her prior 
hospital discharge the decline was thought to be related to the 
PO vancomycin she received for C. diff treatment. Her PCP had 
been trending her counts since discharge, and told the patient 
to be re-admitted when her platelets dropped to 29. CBC on 
admission also notable for white blood cell count of 3.2 and 
hemoglobin 10.2. Plts remained stable throughout hospitalization 
(plts on discharge 24). Hematology was consulted and an 
extensive infectious work-up was unremarkable. Viral studies 
were negative for HCV, HIV, HBV, and EBV. HHV6, MMA, and 
parvovirus were pending on discharge. She did not have 
splenomegaly on prior abdominal imaging so sequestration very 
unlikely. No platelet clumping on smear which was reviewed by 
hematology. There was no laboratory evidence of hemolysis, the 
normal fibrinogen made DIC less likely, there were no 
schistocytes to suggests a microangiopathic process such as TTP, 
and the patient had not had any recent heparin exposure to 
suggest the possibility of HITT. None of her medications were 
likely culprits for thrombocytopenia, so she was continued on 
all home meds (although her cetirizine was held given lack of 
allergic symptoms). A bone marrow biopsy was obtained on ___, 
results pending at discharge. Differential diagnosis at the time 
of discharge included myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) versus 
Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP). The patient was started on a 
trial of prednisone 60mg PO daily on ___. She will have repeat 
CBC on ___. She will be seen by hematology within 1 week of 
discharge. Bone marrow biopsy and CBC results on prednisone will 
be discussed at that visit and it will be decided whether or not 
she should continue steroids. 

CHRONIC, STABLE DIAGNOSES:

# Atrial fibrillation: Warfarin was held on admission to reduce 
bleeding risk. Warfarin should be restarted as soon as platelets 
rise to a safer level, given the patients CHADS-vasc score of 4 
(high risk). She was continued on metoprolol at home dose.

# Pleural Effusion: Likely related to diastolic heart failure 
and moderate-severe mitral regurgitation. Patient was 
asymptomatic throughout her hospitalization. She was continued 
on routine MWF hemodialysis while inpatient.
 
# Anemia: Macrocytic. Definitely a chronic component of 
ESRD-related anemia, but macrocytosis is new this admission. 
Reticulocyte index was elevated which may account for the 
macrocytosis. TSH and B12 were normal. The patient has 
hematology follow-up for further workup of her pancytopenia. 
 
# ESRD: Patient was continued on ___ dialysis. She was continued 
on cinacalcet, midodrine on HD days, nephrocaps, and sevelamer 
TID with meals. 

# Hypothyroidism: TSH was normal. She was continued on home dose 
levothyroxine

# Chronic diastolic CHF: Last echo ___ showed preserved EF. 
Patient appeared euvolemic on exam, except for small pleural 
effusion seen on chest x-ray. She was continued on dialysis, as 
well as a beta blocker.

# Anxiety/insomnia: Stable. Continued on home dose lorazepam 
PRN: anxiety/insomnia

# Reactive Airway Disease: Stable. Continued on 
fluticasone-salmeterol BID, ipratropium PRN, montelukast daily. 
Cetirizine was held given lack of allergic symptoms.

# Arthritis: Continued on gabapentin and lidocaine patches.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure to care for you at ___ 
___. You were admitted with low platelets. We 
performed an extensive work-up including looking for infections 
or medications which can commonly cause low platelets. Thus far, 
the work-up has been unremarkable. The hematology fellow (Dr. 
___ performed a bone marrow biopsy on ___ to look 
for abnormalities in your bone marrow which may be related to 
the problem. In addition, we are starting you on a trial of 
prednisone which will help the hematologists determine if your 
low platelets are caused by a condition called ITP (immune 
thrombocytopenia). You will be called by the hematology office 
with a follow-up appointment within 1 week of discharge. Dr. 
___ will determine if the prednisone is working and 
whether or not you should continue this medication. If you do 
not hear from them by ___ afternoon, please call their 
office at ___ OR email Dr. ___ at 
___. At that hematology appointment they 
will inform you of the results of your bone marrow biopsy. In 
addition, you should have your blood work checked on ___, 
___, with results faxed to Drs. ___ at 
fax # ___.

We STOPPED your warfarin [Coumadin] while you were hospitalized 
to reduce your risk of bleeding. We also emailed your 
cardiologist to let him know about the medication change. You 
should be restarted on warfarin [Coumadin] when your platelet 
count rises to prevent strokes.
  
Given your history of heart failure, weigh yourself every 
morning, call MD if weight goes up more than 3 lbs.
